On this point we differ from the bourgeois “theory of factors,” which arose in the early twentieth century and whose best-known advocate was Max Weber. This theory denies the decisive role of material production in the development of society and places it on the same level as other factors such as geography, the natural environment, population, religion, and so on.↩︎

The cultural remains of the ancient East show a synthetic character in which the language of images and the language of concepts are mixed together—poetry with philosophy, as in Omar Khayyam and al-Ma‘arri, for example. This synthetic character led some Western Orientalists to conclude that philosophy was absent from these Eastern cultural works. But the decisive question is whether categories and concepts are present. Since we do find philosophical views in these works that, despite their synthetic form, take the form of concepts, there is no reason not to classify them as philosophical thought.↩︎

Calling the period before Islam the “Age of Ignorance” is an Islamic usage based on the Qur’anic verse: “When those who disbelieved filled their hearts with zeal—the zeal of the Age of Ignorance” (Qur’an 48:26). As the verse indicates, the word jahiliyya refers to moral conduct, not ignorance as the opposite of knowledge. This is also shown by a report in which Abu Dharr insulted a man in the Prophet’s presence by referring to his mother. The Prophet said to Abu Dharr: “You are a man in whom there is still jahiliyya.” Muslim writers divided jahiliyya into a first jahiliyya, which they said was the age in which Abraham was born, and a second one closer to Islam, in which the Prophet Muhammad was born. The Qatabanian state was contemporary with both the Minaean and Sabaean states, and fell around 525 CE. Its capital stood at the site now known as Kahlan in Wadi Bayhan, near Bab al-Mandab. See al-Sayyid Abd al-Aziz Salim, previous source, p. 140, note 1.↩︎

The Sabaeans fought the Minaean state during its period of weakness until they destroyed it. The Sabaean state then faced internal struggles with tribal chiefs and local rulers seeking power, as well as several local revolts. It also faced external pressures, beginning with the Ptolemies’ attempt in Egypt to monopolize eastern trade and continuing with foreign intervention after internal disorder exhausted the state and weakened its economy. Eventually it lost control of the Red Sea and the African coasts, while maritime trade passed into Greek and Roman hands. The same happened to the Himyarite state. It faced a Roman invasion in 24 BCE, Ethiopian occupation in 340 CE, the diversion of trade from Ma‘rib to the Red Sea maritime route, and the expansion of Roman sea trade. All this led to neglect of the Ma‘rib Dam until it collapsed, followed by migrations and the destruction of agriculture. Same source, pp. 136, 141, 142, 147, 151, 152.↩︎

Zeno held that motion is irrational. He admitted that sensory knowledge tells us motion exists, but he did not accept sensory knowledge as valid. Thought, or rational knowledge, falls into contradiction when it tries to think motion. Motion can be thought only through the contradiction between rest and movement: at a particular point and moment, something both is and is not there. Zeno treated this as a contradiction within thought itself when it thinks motion in this way—that is, as a contradiction according to formal logic. Motion is therefore irrational and, consequently, does not exist. Zeno explained this reasoning through three proofs known as aporias: the arrow, Achilles and the tortoise, and the endless division of a distance into halves while it is being crossed. For these examples, see Ahmad Amin and Zaki Najib Mahmud, The Story of Greek Philosophy, 2nd ed., Cairo, 1935, pp. 46–47.↩︎

To prove that motion is impossible, Zeno imagined an arrow flying through space. At every instant during its flight, he said, the arrow must be at rest at one particular point, because it cannot occupy two places at the same instant. If the arrow is motionless at a particular point during every unit of time, then across the sum of those units it must remain motionless as well. A continuous sequence of states of rest can produce only rest. Therefore there is no motion.↩︎

Zeno tried to deny motion in another way by imagining a man named Achilles racing a tortoise. He assumed that the tortoise begins ten meters ahead and that Achilles runs ten times faster. By the time Achilles covers the ten meters separating them, the tortoise has moved one meter farther. When Achilles covers that meter, the tortoise has moved another tenth of a meter. When he covers that tenth, the tortoise has moved another hundredth of a meter, and so on without end. Achilles therefore never catches the tortoise.↩︎

Evidence for this comes from reports about the kinds of agricultural products brought to the markets of towns and settlements in the Hijaz and elsewhere. Sources tell us, for example, that the towns of the Hijaz—especially Mecca—depended on Ta’if for wheat, other grains, grapes, and honey. See Lammens, The Arab City of Ta’if before the Hijra, Beirut, 1922, p. 32, in French. Ta’if also produced many kinds of fruit, some dates, raisins, figs, and so on. Yaqut al-Hamawi tells us that the seeds of the ban tree produced in Yathrib were carried to other lands. Dictionary of Countries, vol. 5, entry “Yathrib,” p. 87. The point is that these products circulated through markets. Markets were naturally also held during the pilgrimage seasons, and their names are well known. “At these markets Arabs from all parts of the peninsula came with their goods to exchange and sell them” (Salim, p. 364).↩︎
